detail.title: Brain & behaviour basics
detail.tagline: The neuroscience you need for every other topic
tldr: Brain cells talk with chemical messengers. Medicines and therapy both change that talk.
Neurotransmission, circuits and neuroplasticity underlie symptoms, drug action and psychotherapy effects.

sections.title: How cells talk
points: A nerve cell fires an electrical signal
It releases a chemical messenger into the gap (synapse)
The messenger fits receptors on the next cell
The first cell pulls the messenger back in (reuptake)
Reuptake transporters terminate the signal (SSRI target)

sections.title: The main messengers
points: DA: four pathways; antipsychotic and stimulant target
Lost early in Alzheimer's; donepezil boosts it

sections.title: Brain areas
points: Executive function; impaired in ADHD and schizophrenia
Threat detection; overactive in anxiety and PTSD
Declarative memory; shrinks with chronic stress and early Alzheimer's
Controls the HPA axis and circadian rhythm

sections.title: Stress and the body
points: Stress, then brain signal, then hormone chain, then cortisol
Long-term stress affects sleep, memory and mood
Chronic HPA activation linked to depression

sections.title: Why therapy works too
points: Therapy and medicines both change brain activity
Sleep, exercise and connection protect the brain

brain-lateral.title: The brain from the side: lobes, gyri and sulci
brain-lateral.summary: The left side of the brain with the four lobes, the central and lateral sulci, the main gyri, the cerebellum and the brainstem.

labels.name: Frontal lobe
labels.about: Plans, decides, controls impulses and moves the body. Damage changes personality and judgement, as in frontal dementia or a frontal head injury.

labels.name: Superior frontal gyrus
labels.about: The top band of the frontal lobe, part of the planning and self-control network. It holds part of the supplementary motor area near the midline.

labels.name: Middle frontal gyrus
labels.about: Holds much of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, used for working memory and planning. It is the usual target for rTMS in depression.

labels.name: Inferior frontal gyrus
labels.about: The lowest frontal band. On the left side its back part is Broca's area, needed to produce fluent speech.

labels.name: Precentral gyrus
labels.about: The primary motor cortex, which sends the commands for voluntary movement. A stroke here weakens the opposite side of the body.

labels.name: Central sulcus
labels.about: The deep groove between the frontal and parietal lobes, separating movement in front from body sensation behind.

labels.name: Postcentral gyrus
labels.about: The primary somatosensory cortex, which feels touch, pain, temperature and position from the opposite side of the body.

labels.name: Parietal lobe
labels.about: Joins touch, vision and space into a sense of where things and the body are. Right parietal damage can cause neglect of the left side.

labels.name: Supramarginal gyrus
labels.about: Curves around the end of the lateral sulcus. On the left it helps with phonology and repeating words; damage nearby gives conduction aphasia.

labels.name: Angular gyrus
labels.about: Curves around the end of the superior temporal sulcus and links written words to their sounds and meanings. Left damage can cause problems with reading, writing and arithmetic.

labels.name: Lateral sulcus
labels.about: The deep sideways fissure that separates the temporal lobe below from the frontal and parietal lobes above. The insula lies hidden in its depth.

labels.name: Superior temporal gyrus
labels.about: Holds the hearing cortex. On the left its back part is Wernicke's area, needed to understand speech.

labels.name: Temporal lobe
labels.about: Hearing, language understanding, memory and recognising objects and faces. Its inner part holds the hippocampus and amygdala.

labels.name: Occipital lobe
labels.about: The visual cortex. Damage causes loss of part of the field of vision or problems recognising what is seen.

labels.name: Cerebellum
labels.about: Coordinates movement, balance and timing, and helps some thinking. Damage gives an unsteady gait and clumsy hands, as in alcohol misuse.

labels.name: Brainstem
labels.about: Connects the brain to the spinal cord and runs breathing, heart rate, sleep and wakefulness. Damage here can be life threatening.

neuron.title: A neuron and its parts
neuron.summary: A typical motor-type neuron with dendrites, cell body, nucleus, axon hillock, myelinated axon with nodes, and axon terminals.

labels.name: Dendrites
labels.about: Branches that receive messages from other neurons. Their small spines are where most learning changes happen, and they are thinned in chronic stress and depression.

labels.name: Cell body (soma)
labels.about: Holds the nucleus and the machinery that makes proteins and transmitters. It adds up the incoming signals.

labels.name: Nucleus
labels.about: Holds the DNA. Genes switched on here, for example by antidepressants over weeks, change how the cell works.

labels.name: Axon hillock
labels.about: The cone where the axon begins. If the summed input reaches threshold here, the neuron fires an action potential.

labels.name: Axon
labels.about: The long cable that carries the action potential away from the cell body, in some cells for up to a metre.

labels.name: Myelin sheath
labels.about: Fatty insulation wrapped round the axon that makes signals travel much faster. It is lost in multiple sclerosis.

labels.name: Node of Ranvier
labels.about: A short bare gap between sheaths, packed with sodium channels. The signal jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction).

labels.name: Schwann cell nucleus
labels.about: In nerves outside the brain each sheath is one Schwann cell wrapped round the axon, which is why those nerves can regrow after injury.

labels.name: Axon terminals
labels.about: The end branches of the axon, which reach other neurons, muscles or glands.

labels.name: Synaptic bouton
labels.about: The swollen ending that stores transmitter in vesicles and releases it into the synapse.
